_comment: Domains ZUZZ's browser may reach without an extra confirmation prompt.
Strategy (approved Session 10, Q2): start from a preset list of well-known
read-only sites so the first run has zero friction, and treat every domain
that is NOT listed as a confirmation prompt rather than a hard refusal. The
user therefore builds a personalised allowlist by approving domains over
time, and nothing becomes permanently unreachable by accident.
This file is re-read on every lookup, so an edit takes effect without a
server restart. That is also how the Phase 3 UI is expected to add entries:
write into user_added and the next navigation picks it up.
The allowlist is a prompt-removal convenience, NOT a security boundary, in
the same sense as apps_whitelist.json: being listed means 'do not ask', not
'is safe'. A domain that is absent is still reachable after the user
confirms; a domain that is present is still blocked by the entries in
'blocked' below, which always win.
SUPERSEDED — kept only so an older config file still parses.
This key said localhost would be reachable from trust level 5. It is not,
and that was the safer of the two readings rather than the convenient one.
docs/PHASE_3_PLAN.md section 10 tests for a refusal at levels 1-4, which
leaves level 5 open, but 'open' was never the intent: the level-5 escape
hatch would mean that the single configuration in which ZUZZ is trusted to
act alone is also the configuration in which a page it opened can reach
the services running on that machine.
So localhost, 127.0.0.1 and the private ranges are in 'blocked.exact' and
'blocked.private_ranges' below, which the guard applies at every level.
Reach ZUZZ's own local services over the API, where the gate can see the
call, rather than through a page the browser fetched.
Set this to false to confirm you have read this and want it back.
docs/PHASE_3_PLAN.md approved answers, invariant 2: an explicit user command
to go somewhere always asks, even for a domain on the list below.
This is not redundant with 'unknown_domain: ask', because it closes the hole
the allowlist would otherwise open. An allowlist entry means 'do not ask', and
the way that goes wrong is that a URL the user typed by hand — from a link in
an email, a search result, a paste — reads identically to one ZUZZ chose for
itself. Only the first is something the user already said yes to. So when the
request carries the user's own instruction, the list is not consulted for
silence at all.
Set this to false to let ZUZZ act on listed domains without asking even when
the user named the URL. It is a convenience switch, not a safety switch:
everything in 'blocked' still wins regardless.
Phase 3 invariant: JavaScript is enabled on trusted domains and default-denied
on untrusted ones. A preset or user-added domain is trusted; anything else is
not, and until the user confirms it the page runs with scripting off.
The reason this is a separate switch from the allowlist is that a page which
has been confirmed once is a page ZUZZ is now willing to *read*, and reading
is not the same as agreeing to execute whatever it fetches. Turning the
confirmation off and turning the scripting on are two different decisions, and
the UI makes only the first of them.
'ask' is the honest middle: a page that needs scripting runs without it and
ZUZZ says so, so the user is never looking at a blank page wondering what went
wrong.
javascript.on_denied: report that scripting is disabled for this page

_comment: Approved Session 10, Q5: session persistence is per-domain and opt-in. A
domain is written into persist_domains only when the user ticks the box on
that domain, and the 'Forget this domain' button in the UI removes it and
deletes the stored cookies.
The default is a fresh context per session, which means no cookie from one
task is visible to the next. That is the right default for an assistant that
reads the web on the user's behalf: a site that gets a cookie does not get to
keep it, and a task that needs to be logged in asks to be.
Stored state is encrypted at rest with a key generated on this machine on
first use and kept beside the files (storage/sessions/.session.key). The
point is not to defend against the user — it is that a directory of cookies
copied off this laptop by something else should not be a directory of cookies
that still work.
A persisted domain never widens the allowlist: reaching the domain still
needs its own answer.
Caps on what comes back out of a page. A page is attacker-chosen input of
arbitrary length, and an extractor with no cap is a way to fill the context
window with a page's contents before ZUZZ has read a word of the user's
question. Silent truncation is worse than an explicit one, so the extractor
returns a 'truncated' flag alongside the text.
These are deliberately generous. They exist to stop a hostile page, not to
shape ZUZZ's answers — a summary of an article longer than these is a
question for the caller, not a reason for the extractor to hide the article.
extraction.on_truncate: flag it and say how much was dropped

_comment: Never navigable, at any trust level, and not overridable by adding the
domain to user_added. localhost and the private ranges are here because
the browser is the main exfiltration channel out of ZUZZ: a page able to
reach the LAN or the host's own services can post what it read off the
screen to somewhere the allowlist never sees.
169.254.169.254 is the cloud instance-metadata endpoint; reaching it from
a page ZUZZ opened is a credential theft primitive, not a browsing need.
Approved Session 10, Q3: defence in depth. Anything the browser fetches
lands in this isolated directory first and is never written to Desktop.
It is then scored by the Amygdala classifier, and only a confirmed
file is moved anywhere else. The 'quarantine' name is deliberate: it is
not a download folder, it is a holding pen.
A .zip that arrives in quarantine is NOT unpacked, scanned and approved.
That sounds helpful and is exactly the bypass: an archive can contain
setup.exe, and every classification in the list above would wave it
through. So an archive is classified by its extension only, and it stays
in the holding pen until the user does something about it by hand.
The single exception is archives whose whole purpose is to be extracted
by a developer who has a tool for the contents — .zip and .tar.gz and
.whl, the last because pip installs it as a matter of course.
archives_are_not_inspected.on_unknown_archive: quarantine and say the contents were not inspected

_comment: Approved Session 10, Q6: bounded so a runaway loop cannot exhaust RAM/VRAM.
The override is real and it is bounded. 'User can override' would be
meaningless if it meant 'the cap is advisory', so an override is written
down in the audit log with the domain and tab count that justified it, and
it needs its own confirmed web_automation decision rather than the one that
opened the sixth tab.
soft_warning_at is reported to the UI and never blocks. A warning that
blocks is a cap with a worse name.
tabs.on_hard_cap: refuse, and say what the override would cost
